title: Why Your Students Should Read Books, Not Screens
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Observing students staring at screens during independent reading time, Linsin argues against digital reading tools in favor of physical books during that dedicated period. His central claim is that screen-based "reading" — narrated text, animated characters, on-screen assistance — often substitutes passive entertainment for the active decoding and comprehension work that actually builds reading skill, and that research consistently shows physical books outperform screens for fluency and comprehension. He extends the argument psychologically, claiming that students today need physical books as a form of genuine escape, one that lowers rather than raises the stress and anxiety response that screen time is shown to increase. The concrete recommendation is straightforward: keep independent reading time screen-free and lean toward classic literature rather than newer digital-adjacent alternatives. He frames the choice as requiring real courage, since it means pushing back against the pervasive assumption that newer technology is automatically superior, even at the risk of being seen as old-fashioned.
points: Screen-narrated or animated "reading" is described as passive entertainment that substitutes for the decoding work that actually builds skill.
Research is cited as consistently favoring physical books over screens for reading fluency and comprehension.
Physical books are framed as offering genuine psychological escape that lowers, rather than raises, screen-driven stress and anxiety.
Choosing books over trendy technology is framed as requiring real courage to resist the assumption that newer is always better.
quotes: No, they don’t. In fact, any use of technology during independent reading time is a bad idea.
From reading fluency to better comprehension, it’s no comparison. More and more research is showing that old-fashion books are better for kids than the images blue-lighting their faces.
Your students need escape more than any generation before them.
They need healing time away from the metal, glass, and plastic and feel the natural fibers on their fingertips.
But you must have the courage to say no. You must swim against the tide, risk being called a Luddite.
Are screens better at improving reading than actual books? Do they deepen comprehension, speed up fluency, or enhance vocabulary acquisition?
